title: The End of American Innocence
author: Johannes Lichtman

Review

The End of American Innocence

Seventy years after “The Quiet American,” has the country outlived Graham Greene’s prophecy?

August 14, 2026, 2:45 PM

By Johannes Lichtman, the author of Calling Ukraine and Such Good Work.

“[N]othing ages faster than today’s idea of the future,” wrote architecture critic Witold Rybczynski, which may explain why readers treasure the rare novel that correctly predicts what’s to come. The classics of the prescient genre tend be speculative and dystopian—1984, Parable of the Sower, The Handmaid’s Tale—but can also be realist fiction. Take English author Graham Greene’s The Quiet American, published in the United States in 1956, which predicted the future by describing the present.
The Quiet American takes place in 1950s Vietnam, where Ho Chi Minh’s forces are fighting French colonial powers for independence. It’s narrated by Thomas Fowler, a jaded middle-aged British correspondent who has been hiding out from an unhappy marriage for years in Saigon, where he’s involved in a long-term affair with a Vietnamese woman named Phoung. The story’s inciting incident is the arrival of Alden Pyle, an idealistic young member of the “American Economic Mission”—which is to say, he’s a not-very-well-disguised CIA operative—who has come to try to cultivate a U.S.-backed “third force,” neither communist nor colonialist, in Indochina.

The book cover for "The Quiet American" features a pink background covered in an abstract black pattern. Three yellow rectangular blocks overlay the pattern, displaying the title "The Quiet American," the descriptor "a novel," and the author's name "Graham Greene" in dark cursive lettering.
The Quiet American, Graham Greene, Penguin Classics, 208 pp., $18, August 2004, paperback
Fowler is cynical and tired and speaks mainly sarcastic one-liners; Pyle is earnest and eager and illiterate in irony. Pyle falls in love with Phoung, propelling the story’s conflict, which serves as a metaphor for Cold War power struggle. It’s a little strange for a novel about a love triangle in which two of the characters are flat to have such staying power. (Perhaps because of the bias of Fowler’s first-person narration, Phoung exists as little more than metaphor for Vietnam, while Pyle is less an individual than a representative of the United States abroad.) But besides the quiet fury of Greene’s prose, the novel owes its endurance to two main elements.
First, the book anticipated the horror of the U.S. invasion of Vietnam with eerie precision. Pyle’s cultivation of a third force, the dangerous effects of U.S. humanitarian intervention, the catastrophic belief that Vietnam cannot “go” lest all of Asia fall to communism—as historian Kevin Ruane wrote, the novel was “prophetic at the time, uncanny in retrospect.” One of the most chilling scenes occurs when a French pilot describes to Fowler a relatively new weapon that Americans would become very familiar with over the coming years. “What I detest is napalm bombing,” says the pilot. “The poor devils are burnt alive, the flames go over them like water. They are wet through with fire.”

Second, the novel shows the danger of dogmatic faith in American exceptionalism. Pyle sincerely believes in the cultivation of a third force not because it’s good for the United States but because being more like the United States will be good for the Vietnamese. Yet before arriving, he had never been to the country and is basing his entire ideology on the writing of a U.S. political scientist, who, as Greene puts it, is the type of thinker that “gets hold of an idea and then alters every situation to fit the idea.” The climax of the novel comes when the third force that Pyle has financed on behalf of the CIA sets off a bomb in a crowded Saigon market, killing and wounding civilians. Fowler, after watching a mother cover the body of her dead infant with her hat, is shaking with fury when he finds Pyle, who, never having seen death before, is in a state of shock at the sight of blood on his shoe. By evening, Pyle has found his wits and neatly explains away the murders without needing to change his beliefs at all: “It was a pity, but you can’t always hit your target.”
Pyle does not plot to kill civilians. Yet when the people he naively put his faith in do the killing, he assimilates the act into his worldview with a simple conjunction: “but.” He adds of the murdered women and children, “In a way you could say they died for democracy.”
“He’ll always be innocent,” Fowler thinks. “Innocence is a kind of insanity.” So Fowler decides to tip off the communists to Pyle’s location, signing the American’s death sentence. “I am not altogether sorry,” says a French police officer after Pyle’s body is discovered. “He was doing a lot of harm.”

Rows of white headstones stretch across the rolling grounds of Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia, on May 25, 2025.Probal Rashid/LightRocket via Getty Images
The only quiet American, Greene seems to suggest, is a dead American.
In the years after publication, Greene’s portrait of a man determined “to do good, not to any individual person but to a country, a continent, the world” has been used to explain the attitude behind not only the U.S. invasion of Vietnam, but countless foreign interventions, including the so-called forever wars of the 2000s, in which the declining U.S. empire was determined to spread democracy and freedom no matter how many people it had to kill along the way.
But on the 70th anniversary of the book’s stateside publication, I wonder: Does The Quiet American, which warns of the danger of American innocence, still have anything to say about the United States in 2026, or has the country outlived Greene’s prophecy?

A person holds up a cardboard sign with handwritten text in support of military action in the foreground. In the background, a person in a blue hooded jacket stands near a waving American flag with a large brick building behind them.
An unidentified man walks between a sign and a U.S. flag during a rally in support of the Iraq War, in Hartford, Connecticut, on April 5, 2003.Bob Falcetti/Getty Images

When The Quiet American was published in the United Kingdom in 1955, it was a sensation, but the U.S. reception the following year was not enthusiastic. The New Yorker ran an infamously mocking review, and across the press, Greene was accused of shallow stereotyping, anti-Americanism, and communism. Most galling for Greene was the 1958 Hollywood adaption of the novel, which recast Pyle as the hero of the story and Fowler as the gullible European. (The Quiet American had the rare distinction of garnering dramatic adaptions in both the United States and the Soviet Union, where it was staged at a Moscow theater. The former incensed Greene, who called it “pure treachery” and “a deliberate travesty”; the latter made less of an impression, though he did remark in a letter from 1960 that the Soviet production was “very bad.”)

To be fair to the critics who accused him of anti-Americanism, Greene did not like the United States. “I would go to any lengths to put my feeble twigs into the spokes of American foreign policy,” he once said. Starting in the early 1950s and up until his death in 1991, Greene would publicly criticize the United States for its disastrous interventions in Vietnam, Haiti, and Latin America. He would also, following publication of The Quiet American, be surveilled by U.S. intelligence, who spied on him and read his mail.

But this distaste wasn’t because, or at least not primarily because, he was jealous of the U.S. empire supplanting the British, as Greene’s U.S. critics suggested. Nor was his devastating portrait of Pyle based on stereotypes about Americans from movies. Instead, it derived from U.S. conduct abroad; Pyle, though not a particularly three-dimensional character, was based on the Americans that Greene’s extensive travels allowed him to meet.
In The Quiet American, Fowler tells Pyle, “I don’t like Ike.” In U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower, Fowler sees not postwar prosperity but repression of freedom domestically and domino theory-inspired bloodshed abroad. Referencing McCarthyism, he says that Pyle’s children will surely grow up to be “bright young American citizens ready to testify.” He mocks Pyle as a virgin, both sexually and spiritually—a crewcut young man who can think of no higher compliment than calling someone “swell.”
Whether or not Greene’s portrayal of Pyle is inaccurate, as Greene’s U.S. critics claimed, the character is an accurate representation of U.S. foreign policy during the Cold War, when the CIA was finding its footing as a disruptor of any left-wing movement around the globe, no matter how democratic.

A group of young men in military fatigues sit at wooden school desks arranged in rows under an open-sided outdoor pavilion. They look forward toward an instructor whose shoulder and back are seen in the right foreground. Some desks have notebooks resting on them, and a rifle is propped against one of the chairs.
A U.S. Army trainer, attached to the U.S. Military Group in El Salvador, speaks to a class of Salvadoran Army soldiers, in San Miguel Department, El Salvador, in August 1984.Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images
Despite its initial reception, The Quiet American grew in popularity in the United States during the Vietnam War. David Halberstam said that the novel was, for war correspondents, “our bible.” Robert Stone estimated that “every experienced American commentator on Vietnam to one degree or another admires The Quiet American.” It has remained a part of the U.S. national consciousness ever since. Last year, Ruane suggested in Jacobin that the novel is “no less resonant today with a distinctly un-quiet American in the White House.”
But it’s hard not to feel that the novel has, in reality, finally become outdated. The Quiet American suggests that the United States’ greatest sin is its innocence. Innocence, in the case of Pyle, is the belief that what you do is right because you do it. You are good, so your actions must be in service of good. When bad things happen, it isn’t because your cause is bad—it is because mistakes were made, and these were exceptions to the rule of goodness. Besides, badness in the service of goodness can always be excused with a simple conjunction; as I remember hearing an adult say during my adolescence, after the Abu Ghraib torture pictures leaked: “I don’t condone it, but sometimes soldiers need to let off steam.”

A soldier in full military gear stands guard in an open doorway of a building behind a chain-link fence topped with razor wire. The metal gate in the fence stands open in the foreground, and several upper windows of the building are covered with plywood panels.
A U.S. soldier maintains security at the Abu Ghraib prison in Abu Ghraib, Iraq, on May 10, 2004.Khampha Bouaphanh/Getty Images
Now, under President Donald Trump, the U.S. government no longer pretends to even care about the ideals of freedom and democracy. U.S. foreign policy in 2026 isn’t, as Fowler said of Pyle, armored by good intentions and ignorance; it’s armored by bad intentions (greed, revenge, and self-promotion) and ignorance. The White House simply wants the best deals for the United States—a perverse reverse synecdoche in which the United States now means the president. In a world where Russian President Vladimir Putin is just as good a partner for Washington as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, a world in which the U.S. president gleefully threatens to wipe out an entire civilization for not doing what he says, the catastrophe of U.S. innocence has given way to the evil of U.S. cynicism.
I doubt that The Quiet American will retain its canonical status if the United States continues on its current path. As prophetic as the novel proved for 60-some years after its publication, the fact that two of three main characters aren’t particularly interesting as people may become more of a problem if their metaphorical purpose is less urgent. Of course, that prediction could prove moot if Washington returns to a foreign policy that, as Greene said, has the best intentions for all the trouble it causes. But the future is notoriously difficult to predict.
